questions.q: Why should training loss, gradient norm, learning rate, and throughput all be logged together rather than any one substituting for the others?
options: Because only one of these metrics is ever useful, and the rest are redundant
Because each metric can look healthy while another degrades -- for example, loss can appear fine while throughput quietly drops due to a straggler -- so no single metric tells the whole story
Because training frameworks require exactly four metrics to be logged by law
Because logging fewer than four metrics causes the training job to crash
questions.explain: These metrics capture different failure modes -- a straggler shows up in throughput, instability shows up in gradient norm -- so logging only one risks missing problems the others would reveal.

questions.q: What does model FLOPs utilization (MFU) measure that raw tokens-per-second throughput does not?
options: The total number of parameters in the model
Achieved compute as a fraction of the GPU hardware's theoretical peak FLOPs, revealing whether the hardware is being used efficiently relative to its ceiling
The exact dollar cost of the training run
The number of GPUs currently connected to the cluster
questions.explain: MFU normalizes achieved throughput against the model's size and the hardware's theoretical peak FLOPs, showing how efficiently the available compute is being used -- something raw tokens/sec alone doesn't reveal.

questions.q: What is the distinction between training-metric observability (via tools like Weights & Biases) and cluster-level observability (via DCGM/Prometheus/Grafana)?
options: There is no distinction -- they measure exactly the same thing

Training metrics answer whether the model is learning well (loss, grad norm, MFU), while cluster-level metrics answer whether the hardware itself is healthy (GPU temperature, ECC errors, network status)
Cluster-level observability only applies to single-GPU training
Training metrics can only be viewed by the model's original author
questions.explain: Training metrics track learning progress and model behavior, while cluster-level metrics track the physical health of the hardware -- a separate layer that often surfaces problems like stragglers before they cause a crash.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that alerting matters more than dashboards alone?
options: Dashboards are never useful for training runs
A dashboard nobody is watching during an off-hours incident (like a 3 a.m. loss spike) doesn't help -- automated alerts pull a human in immediately rather than relying on someone noticing later
Alerts replace the need for any metric logging at all
Alerting is only possible with Weights & Biases and no other tool
questions.explain: A dashboard only helps if someone is actively watching it; automated alerts on thresholds (loss spikes, gradient norm spikes, MFU drops) ensure a human is notified immediately regardless of when the problem occurs.

questions.q: Why does gradient norm matter as a logged metric during training?
options: It has no relationship to training stability and is logged only for historical record-keeping
A sudden spike in gradient norm often precedes or accompanies loss spikes and training instability, making it an early warning signal
Gradient norm determines the exact number of GPUs needed for the job
Gradient norm is only relevant during inference, not training
questions.explain: A spike in gradient norm is a signal often associated with instability or an impending loss spike, making it a useful early-warning metric alongside loss itself.
